item.title: Choking Global Trade
item.description:
To get from Minnesota to China, a load of soybeans might meander down the Mississippi River on a barge, transferring around New Orleans to a ship that carries it through the Panama Canal and across the Pacific.

But this summer, low water levels have throttled traffic moving through the canal and limited barge cargo on the river. In Europe, the Rhine and Danube rivers, both important shipping channels, also saw record-low water levels.

Across the logistics industry, it’s been a season of bottlenecks caused by low rainfall and shrinking rivers.

In addition to the heat, floods and storms that have delivered acute shocks to local economies in recent months, climate change is worsening droughts, increasing shipping costs and slowing movement through the waterways that act as conveyor belts for global trade. Add in record-setting prices for the diesel that powers the global cargo industry, and it’s no wonder costs of goods are climbing.

“I think the combination of factors probably, either now or soon, will be fairly significant in terms of increasing world food costs,” said David Gantz, a fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy.

About 5 percent of ocean shipping traffic flows through the Panama Canal, which relies on a system of locks that use millions of gallons of fresh water to move ships. Low rainfall, made worse by El Niño weather patterns, has contributed to low water levels in the lakes that feed the canal. The authorities have responded by slashing the number of vessels that can travel through the waterway each day.

At the start of the month, the number of slots available fell from 38 to 34. Next week, it will be cut to 32.

This is not the first time a drought has affected shipments through the Panama Canal. In 2023, severe water shortages pushed daily transits down to 24 per day.

On the Mississippi River, which carries the barges that transport almost half of U.S. corn and soybean exports, the American Commercial Barge Line implemented its low-water protocol this month, setting limits on how low vessels can sit on certain parts of the river. That means operators have to lighten their loads or use smaller boats.

Low water levels in the Mississippi have caused problems off and on for several years now, Gantz said. The waterway offers a cost-effective means of transporting agricultural goods from the Corn Belt to the Gulf Coast. A single barge can carry the equivalent of more than a thousand trucks or 200 rail cars, according to the American Farm Bureau.

The most severe Mississippi River drought on record came in 2022, when reduced capacity and delayed shipments drove up the costs of transport and ultimately drove agricultural exports from Louisiana ports down by almost 4 percent, according to an analysis by researchers at North Dakota State University.

The Rhine River, one of Europe’s main shipping arteries, hit all-time lows this year, exposing sunken ships and forcing barge operators to lighten their loads. The drought fell outside of typical periods of low flow, which have historically happened in the fall. A 2018 drought that affected the Rhine shaved 0.3 percent off Germany’s economic output that year.

“We’re seeing this kind of water crisis a lot earlier than normally we would expect to be dealing with it,” said Alexandra Naegele, research scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center.

Woodwell’s projections suggest that in the next few decades, the Rhine could see two additional weeks per year when water levels fall so low that barges have to reduce their volume by at least half.

While shrinking rivers are paralyzing traditional trade routes, warmer temperatures are opening new ones in the summer months as Arctic sea ice disappears. Just this week, a Chinese cargo ship, the Dubai Tower, finished a three-week journey from Qingdao to Teesport, England, using an Arctic shortcut that shaved several days off the trip from Asia to Europe.

It’s a major milestone and an indicator of the big changes to come as a warming planet redraws shipping routes, but experts say it’s not yet commercially feasible.

One major hurdle: The season doesn’t last long before the ice freezes over. The shipping company behind Dubai Tower is hoping to sail seven more times before winter sets in.

A group representing more than 800 former employees of the Environmental Protection Agency today sounded the alarm over the health consequences of data centers. It warned that Trump administration policies to weaken pollution safeguards and speed up approvals of data centers threatened to increase health risks across the country.

In a report set to publish Thursday, the nonprofit Environmental Protection Network examined projected pollution from the power plants, gas turbines and diesel generators needed to meet data centers’ surging electricity demand.

“These are decisions that can affect what Americans breathe, what gets into our water and, ultimately, what can make its way into our soil and food supply,” said Dr. Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and former E.P.A. assistant administrator who is a member of the group. — Hiroko Tabuchi

item.title: Rubio Talks of Cooperating With Peru on Crime Crackdown
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday that the United States would work with the new leader of Peru to crack down on organized crime groups in the country, but gave no details on any plans for cooperation.

Mr. Rubio spoke about the potential partnership in general terms after a meeting with Keiko Fujimori, the recently elected conservative president of Peru.

At a news conference with Mr. Rubio, she said her country had joined the Shield of the Americas, a coalition of Latin American nations mostly led by conservative leaders that was organized by the Trump administration.

The stated aim of the coalition, which has more than a dozen members, is to work together to crack down on organized crime in the Western Hemisphere. Mr. Rubio announced in writing before his trip to South America this week that Peru was joining the coalition.

“These are transnational terrorist organizations that do not respect sovereign borders,” he said on Thursday of crime groups. “We’re going to help as much as we possibly can, because it’s in our national interests as well.”

Ms. Fujimori, who promised during her campaign to end a surge in crime, said, “For us who have had to face terrorism, we know how difficult it is now to confront this crime that does not respect borders, and that is why there is the need to join efforts with other countries.”

In the 1980s, the Peruvian government fought the Shining Path, a Maoist insurgency, but that group operated only in Peru.

Mr. Rubio’s message was consistent with an increasingly militarized approach by the Trump administration to Latin America. It is carrying out attacks and pushing for governments in the region to accede to working with the U.S. military on operations within their countries.

Mr. Rubio’s State Department has designated certain Latin American crime groups foreign terrorist organizations to limit their access to financial resources and to help justify U.S. military operations, though the designation does not give the government a legal basis for such operations.

“We’re not going to do anything that our partners don’t ask us to do,” Mr. Rubio said when asked whether the Trump administration might take unilateral military action in the countries.

Mr. Rubio’s meeting with Ms. Fujimori on Thursday came on the third and final stop of a trip this week across Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, with regional security a main talking point in each country.

Mr. Rubio and other top Trump administration officials aim to bolster political ties with conservative figures and administrations in Latin America. And since early 2025, Mr. Rubio has been pressing those governments to work with the U.S. military and other federal agencies on operations against gangs and crime groups, in particular those involved in drug trafficking.

In Barranquilla, Colombia, Mr. Rubio spoke with the country’s new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, about security and economic cooperation. The same issues were the focus of Mr. Rubio’s meeting with Daniel Noboa, the president of Ecuador, in that country’s capital, Quito, on Wednesday. The Pentagon has been working with the militaries in both countries, though one operation in Ecuador resulted in the bombing of a dairy farm and the abuse of its workers, The New York Times reported.

In Ms. Fujimori, the daughter of a former president, the Trump administration has another potential right-wing ally.

Ms. Fujimori took office on July 28 on promises to wield an iron fist to restore order amid a wave of extortion rackets and hired killings that prey on small businesses and the working poor. As a candidate Ms. Fujimori leaned heavily into the legacy of her father, late authoritarian leader Alberto Fujimori, who oversaw the capture of the leader of the Shining Path but was later imprisoned for human rights violations committed during a bloody counterinsurgency campaign when he governed from 1990 to 2000.

Transnational drug cartels working in Ecuador and Colombia do not have a notable presence in Peru. That country is the world’s second-largest producer of cocaine, with most of it smuggled to Brazil and Europe. But the recent surge in crime has been driven by hundreds of gangs that deal in extortion, illegal mining, human trafficking and kidnapping.

One of the most notorious criminal groups in Peru, Los Pulpos, has expanded into neighboring countries.

On Sept. 1, in a joint operation with two U.S. agencies, the F.B.I. and the D.E.A., the authorities in Bolivia captured the group’s leader, Jhonsson Cruz. Ms. Fujimori hailed that cooperation on Thursday, saying it showed how international partnerships could produce concrete results in the fight against transnational crime.

The U.S. government has also tried to get Peru to back away from aspects of its partnership with China, the country’s largest trade partner. Some U.S. officials are especially concerned about a Chinese-built port in the city of Chancay.

When asked by a reporter about relations with China, Ms. Fujimori said that Peru was part of an Asia-Pacific trade coalition, and that “we will continue this effort of having trade exchanges with different countries from Asia, from the Pacific and from Europe.”

item.title: Hobbyist Archaeologist Uncovers Finland’s Largest Viking-Age Coin Hoard
item.description:
A metal detectorist in southern Finland searching for treasure in the forest of his hometown this month uncovered what professional archaeologists say is the largest Viking-Age silver coin hoard ever found in the country.

The Lahti Museums, which manages archaeological heritage in Sysma, where the hoard was found, credited the detectorist, Kalle Lappinen, with leading archaeologists to a collection of thousands of coins and other silver objects. They include a bracelet and a silver bead, the museum said in a statement on Wednesday.

The museum inspected and recovered the hoard after Mr. Lappinen alerted the antiquities authorities. Now it plans to clean, study and date the discoveries precisely, it said.

There are about 10 pounds of coins, according to its initial assessment, double the size of a collection found in 1895 in Nousiainen that contained 1,700 coins.

The new discovery is “very significant” and shines a light on Finland’s link to the Vikings, said Toni Paukku, an archaeologist at the Lahti Museums.

The Viking Age, from roughly 750 to 1050, coincides with a period in the late Finnish Iron Age. Vikings lived in what is now Sweden, Norway and Denmark. The new find underlines that “Finland was strongly connected to the Scandinavian cultural sphere, boosted by the trade of Scandinavian seafarers — some of whom were indeed Vikings — across the Baltic Sea,” Mr. Paukku said in an email.

The treasures were found packed in the remains of two birch bark containers, and buried about 18 inches underground.

“Intentionally hidden treasures like these are somewhat common for this era in Finland,” said Mr. Paukku, pointing to the societal unrest tied to general instability and external threats. Religious traditions prevalent at the time may also have played a role, with many then believing that buried riches could follow a person into the afterlife, he noted.

But precisely why this particular stash was buried is unclear, Mr. Paukku said. “One can only say that whoever they were, they did not come back to collect the treasure,” he said. “No burials appear to be associated with the hoard.”

Mr. Lappinen, the detectorist who discovered the treasure, said he had searched in the area on other occasions but failed to find anything until returning to it earlier this month. After getting a couple of signals, he began digging until his pinpointer — a small hand-held probe — “roared,” he said in an email.

“With the fury of a monkey, I dug through the soil, bottom moraine and cobblestones,” Mr. Lappinen said. At a depth of about 18 inches, he said, he found “a pile of coins” and then reported it to the authorities — after he “recovered from the adrenaline rush.”

Then he realized there was more to discover.

“It started to crackle,” Mr. Lappinen said of his detector. When he looked, he found more coins in “two hoards side by side.”

Mr. Lappinen, 40, works as an officer in the merchant navy and has a side business as a dealer in antique tiled stoves. His mother, he said, is a history buff — she was delighted by the discovery — and he has been tracking down historical treasures since 1998.

He previously discovered a smaller Viking-Age silver hoard and a collection of Swedish copper plate money, among other treasures. Still, Mr. Lappinen was initially dubious when he made the latest discovery.

The discovery shows that “detectorists can produce a considerable amount of new valuable information about the past, not the least because they (as in this case) search in areas that professional archaeologists do not go to,” an archaeologist at the University of Helsinki, Eljas Oksanen, said in an email.

Mr. Oksanen has written about the risks and benefits of hobbyists making historically important finds.

Hobbyist metal detecting can be controversial in archaeological circles. It raises the risk that an important site may not be properly preserved for study, Mr. Oksanen and a fellow archaeologist, Anna Wessman of the University Museum of Bergen in Norway, wrote last year in the journal Internet Archaeology.

But much new archaeological information has come to light in the last decade thanks to detectorists, Mr. Oksanen said, “transforming” archaeologists’ understanding of the Late Iron Age. Remains of the birch-bark containers in which the coins had been placed may also yield valuable information and are rarely found in Finland’s highly acidic soils, he said, making the latest hoard “a doubly rare find!”

Hobbyists are expected to follow the guidelines set by Finnish Heritage Agency, Mr. Oksanen noted. He lauded Mr. Lappinen’s decision to immediately alert the authorities, saying this appeared to be “a case of responsible and responsive detecting, which has produced a promising archaeological discovery.”

Mr. Lappinen, for his part, says he is highly cognizant of the responsibility that comes with his hobby and is delighted by his latest archaeological contribution. “It was extremely nice to prove with this hoard that my hometown, Sysma, has been something really special during the Viking Age,” he said.

item.title: Bayeux Mania
item.description:
My adopted home country of Britain is gripped by “Bayeux mania.” Everyone wants to see the Bayeux Tapestry, an epic embroidery, nearly 70 meters long, that went on display at the British Museum yesterday.

The tapestry itself is remarkable. Made almost 1,000 years ago, it tells the story of a pivotal moment in British history: The bloody Battle of Hastings, in which William the Conqueror, the Duke of Normandy, defeated Harold Godwinson, England’s last Anglo-Saxon king, laying the foundation for many aspects of modern Britain.

But another source of excitement is simply that it’s here. How was it moved from France? Very, very carefully. Today my colleague Alex Marshall writes about what its improbable journey might mean for other supposedly immovable priceless works of art.

by Alex Marshall

When Emmanuel Macron of France first announced he’d loan the Bayeux Tapestry to Britain, in 2018, I had a thought: That isn’t going to happen.

Napoleon might once have shifted the embroidery, which depicts the Norman invasion of Britain, from its home in Bayeux, along bumpy roads to the Louvre in Paris. But in 1803, who was going to argue with him?

The Nazis also managed to shift the tapestry around France — ultimately hoping to steal it away to Germany — but few were going to resist them, either.

In 2018, Macron didn’t have the power of Napoleon, or the Nazis, and I thought he would struggle to overcome objections from the tapestry’s conservators, who said the tapestry was too fragile to leave its hometown, let alone travel to Britain, where the embroidery was made.

I was wrong. Eight years later, the tapestry is in the British Museum in London, the centerpiece of the most eagerly anticipated museum show of the year, which opened yesterday and runs through July 11.

The artifact’s high-security move proves that conservation science has developed to the point where an object once thought immovable can cross borders. And that raises an intriguing question: If it’s now safe to move the tapestry, surely it’s safe to shift other supposedly immovable priceless objects, too?

16,445 wrinkles, 9,646 holes and 30 tears

The Bayeux Tapestry is not a sturdy object. A 2020 study found it had 16,445 wrinkles, 9,646 holes and 30 tears, among other damage. After Macron’s 2018 announcement, numerous conservators expressed their horror.

So what changed? The conservators I spoke to said a main difference was that they could now work with scientists and engineers to model the vibrations that might occur during transport, then develop methods to limit them. And in this case, they had the financial backing to do such work properly.

For its move to Britain, about 100 technicians carefully put the tapestry into a crate, then a climate-controlled case suspended in a spring-mounted cage. The huge springs surrounding that cage are sometimes used in earthquake zones, and have in recent years been used to move other fragile artworks including valuable pastels, sculptures and paintings.

The technology isn’t perfect. Thalia Bajon-Bouzid, one of the tapestry’s conservators, said in an email last week that the tapestry arrived in Britain with two thread breaks, a few millimeters long. Still, she said, there was “no major visible damage.”

Should a museum want to move a supposedly-immovable masterpiece, there is now more evidence that this is possible. It also has more evidence that doing so can reap huge rewards.

The return of the blockbuster exhibition?

The strange thing about the British Museum exhibition is that such blockbusters were meant to be a thing of the past. Around the time of the coronavirus pandemic, some European museum leaders, faced with plunging visitor numbers and a tough financial environment said it was becoming too expensive to ship masterpieces around the world for mega-exhibitions.

Those comments now seem premature. The British Museum’s show isn’t even the only blockbuster exhibition in London this fall. In November, the National Gallery will open a show of work by the Dutch master Jan van Eyck bringing together all nine of his painted portraits “for the first time in history.”

Blockbuster exhibitions almost always require that objects travel. Those van Eyck paintings will come from Berlin, Bruges, Vienna and Sibiu in Romania, as well as the museum’s own collections. “Only once, only at the National Gallery,” the show’s marketing goes.

So if more objects can be moved safely than ever before, are we about to enter a new era of blockbusters, with priceless art crisscrossing the globe? Could Picasso’s “Guernica” leave Madrid for the first time in over 40 years? Will Michelangelo’s David, which not even World War II could move from its home in Florence, suddenly pop up in New York? Is the Mona Lisa OK to travel the world again, as it did in the 1960s and 1970s?

Perhaps we’re one step closer. But it’s not just conservators who have to agree. Museums have to be willing to let their artworks go, too, and many would still prefer to keep their masterpieces to themselves. One key reason the tapestry could move to Britain was that its home in Bayeux is closed for refurbishment.

The Louvre, for one, is not going to give up its masterpieces easily. When I recently contacted it about the possibility of Da Vinci’s Mona Lisa going out on loan again, a spokeswoman acknowledged recent scientific advances, but said they didn’t eliminate the potential for vibrations entirely. The Mona Lisa’s backing panel is cracked, she added, so sending the painting outside the Louvre would risk it splitting in two.

No one would want that, of course. Unless, that is, a French president decides the risk is worth taking after all.

New York City will hold a solemn ceremony today commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks.

Across the country, it’s been a time of reflection as Americans navigate the legacy of that day. Did 9/11 change everything? A quarter-century on, it is possible to consider the question with some critical distance, Charles Homans writes in The New York Times Magazine. The day’s influence is not as singular as it might have once seemed. It’s a “middle chapter in the story of American fracture rather than the pyrotechnic beginning,” he writes.

Al Qaeda now: The Taliban claim Afghanistan is no longer a sanctuary for terrorist groups, but Al Qaeda and others are still present.

President Trump said he would give $5,000 checks to every American adult if his party keeps control of Congress in the November elections. The proposal, like many others, may not come to pass.

Trump’s Republican Party is holding a convention this week that looks more like a rally ahead of the midterm elections. But some candidates are staying away. Maggie Haberman explains in this video.

The Houthis in Yemen captured the port city of Mokha, in an offensive that could give the militia greater control over an important Red Sea shipping route.

At least five people died and more than 80 were missing after a fire on a passenger ferry in the Philippines.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about Apple’s new foldable iPhone Duo.

It was one of Princess Diana’s most enduring fashion statements. She wore the black cocktail dress to a party in London on the same day that Prince Charles, now king, obliquely admitted to an affair on national television. The so-called “revenge dress” is expected to fetch up to $300,000 at auction.

Wildfire smoke has been so severe in Malaysia in recent weeks that officials are trying to make rain to improve air quality.

The authorities recently sent a large transport plane to areas near the Indonesian border to find the perfect clouds for seeding. The crew sprayed a saltwater solution that helps droplets merge and fall as rain. Malaysian officials said the operation improved air quality, but scientists are divided about how effective cloud seeding really is. Read more and see the special aircraft.

Wow. So many of you replied to my question about European identity. Thank you. It was by far the biggest response we’ve ever had. That itself is telling.

The other notable thing to me is the discrepancy between the personal affinity with Europe most of you describe, and the frustration with the E.U. many feel.

Ahead of next week’s State of the Union address by the president of the European Commission, I want to share some of your comments (Ursula, I hope you’re reading).

For some of you, the feeling of being European actually trumps a sense of national identity. Britta Pulz-Fröhlich feels Schleswig-Holsteiner first (“This is my home, my culture and my people”) and European second. “Funnily, I don’t really feel a ‘German’ identity,” she writes; she has more in common with Danes just across the border than Bavarians 700 kilometers south.

Britta’s Europe is one where regions rather than nations blend into one another, giving “a gradual change of cultures geographically from north to south and east to west, which in the end still just feel like different flavors of ‘European,’ in Finland (Europe with cold weather) as much as in Portugal (Europe with warm weather).”

I love this.

To some, Europe’s freedom of movement — the ability to live and work in 27 different countries — is convenient rather than identity-forging: Richard Funke, who lives in Belgium with an Italian partner, said cross-border mobility had taken away the “foreignness,” but he doesn’t think “this makes people suddenly proud Europeans.”

I also sensed some complicated feelings from eastern European readers. Genika Grigorova from Bulgaria fears that some economic and cultural divides between east and west are “unbridgeable.” They “always remind you that you are not really a part of Europe,” she wrote.

I think you are! And to reinforce that message, here’s “Habibi” by Azis, Bulgaria’s king of pop-folk.

Have a great weekend! — Katrin

item.title: Toyohiro Akiyama, Japan’s Chain-Smoking ‘Space Antihero,’ Dies at 84
item.description:
Toyohiro Akiyama, a television reporter who became the first Japanese person to enter space, earning the nickname “space antihero” for his lack of bravura and insatiable cigarette cravings, died on Aug. 26 at his home in Odai, Japan, about 85 miles southeast of Kyoto. He was 84.

The cause was lower gastrointestinal bleeding, his wife, Reiko, said.

In 1990, at the end of the Cold War, Mr. Akiyama became the star of an improbable reality show, broadcast live before millions, when he was sent by his network, the Tokyo Broadcasting System, on a commercial voyage to the Mir space station alongside two Soviet cosmonauts. It was a spectacular $35 million ratings stunt, with TBS paying about half that amount directly to the Soviet Union to include Mr. Akiyama, then 48, in the launch. And it would make him the first journalist to go to space.

It seemed plausible that Mr. Akiyama would return a national hero. Instead, he was wracked by nausea and discomfort on the eight-day mission; his Soviet colleagues later said they had never seen a man vomit so much.

Mr. Akiyama devoted his broadcasts from the cosmos to stories about headaches, bland food and complicated bathroom protocols, and they contained no grand revelations or meditations on the meaning of life. A chain smoker, he frequently pined for cigarettes — and for natto, the fermented beans of his home country.

The voyage did not turn out to be the ratings hit that his network expected. But Mr. Akiyama earned his place in history as an unlikely journeyman, inspiring some of Japan’s first professional astronauts.

He became known for his plain-spoken narration from the heavens, including his first words from space — “Is this live?” — broadcast as he was strapped to a wall to keep stable.

While Mr. Akiyama vowed never to return to space — “I don’t particularly want to see it again, it’s not a very fun place,” he later said — he emerged changed by the experience and eventually devoted himself to organic farming.

“The Earth looked so beautiful from space,” he said in a 2021 interview with the public broadcaster NHK. “I felt a message from nature. The starry sky and the darkness of space — it made me think about how I should live after returning to Earth.”

Mr. Akiyama was born on July 22, 1942, in Tokyo, the youngest of three children. His father, Kanichi Akiyama, was a pharmacist who was dispatched to Malaysia during World War II, and his mother, Kiyo, managed the home.

His upbringing was difficult; his parents often fought, he recalled in a 1992 biography by the journalist Takashi Tachibana, especially after his father lost his job. Young Mr. Akiyama was shy and sometimes feigned illness to skip class.

Still, he had an aptitude for Japanese and English, and in 1966 he graduated from International Christian University in Tokyo and joined TBS, one of Japan’s most prominent broadcasters.

He rose through the ranks, despite gaining a reputation as an aggressive and sometimes hotheaded reporter, prone to slamming down the phone. He spent several years working for the BBC World Service in London before returning to TBS in 1971.

In 1984, he was named the network’s Washington bureau chief. A breakthrough came the next year, when he outmaneuvered other foreign journalists to land an interview with President Ronald Reagan.

“I was captivated by the thrill of live television broadcasting,” he later said, “encountering raw reality and conveying the scene directly to viewers just as it was.”

In 1988, to celebrate its 40th anniversary, TBS came up with the far-fetched idea of sending an employee to space. At the time, Japan was an emerging superpower, and its economy was at its peak before entering three decades of stagnation. It was also the heyday of broadcasting, and TBS, flush with cash, was eager to make a name on the global stage.

The network received more than 100 applications. Mr. Akiyama was initially disqualified because of stomach ulcers, but he protested. “Is there anyone who worked at a television station until the age of 46 and didn’t have ulcers in their stomach?” he told network executives, according to a 2018 interview.

Ultimately, TBS settled on Mr. Akiyama, and he was sent to Star City, an astronaut training ground near Moscow, where he learned to fly on Russian Soyuz spacecraft for about a year. He was joined by the runner-up in the contest, a videographer named Ryoko Kikuchi, who would serve as an alternate. (A week before the launch, Ms. Kikuchi was sidelined because of emergency surgery to treat acute appendicitis.)

Ms. Kikuchi recalled in an interview the exhaustion that she and Mr. Akiyama felt undergoing rigorous training sessions conducted entirely in Russian. The instructors initially forbade students from taking home textbooks, saying they were classified. Then Mr. Akiyama intervened, sparring loudly with the staff until they reversed course.

“It was incredibly grueling — studying subjects outside our expertise,” Ms. Kikuchi said, “and doing it all in Russian.”

On Dec. 2, 1990, Mr. Akiyama and two cosmonauts boarded the Soyuz TM-11 spacecraft, which was covered in advertisements for TBS and other Japanese companies. From space, he described Earth as “really blue,” and said the seas around Japan were “very muddy,” suggesting they were polluted. He said his home country looked like it had “moss all over,” except for the northern island of Hokkaido, which he said looked like “delicious kelp.”

He was sometimes so absorbed by the beauty of the rising sun and passing clouds, he later said, that he forgot to capture key shots — angering some viewers back home.

Aboard the Mir, he reported on the movements in zero gravity of six green Japanese tree frogs that he had brought on board, part of an experiment for Japanese schoolchildren. (Fat frogs, he contended, loved the feeling of weightlessness.)

His brain, he complained, felt as if it were “floating around in my head.” Told to pack light, he did not bring enough underwear, he confessed in his reports.

Ratings at TBS initially surged, but viewership soon leveled off, with most people tuning out after about 10 minutes, according to data at the time. At one point, eager to cheer up his audience, Mr. Akiyama shared footage of Mount Fuji, a white speck.

There was also resentment at home that Mr. Akiyama was the first Japanese national in space — rather than a professional astronaut like Mamoru Mohri, who had trained at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. (Mr. Mohri had been set to make history as the first Japanese citizen in space, but his mission was delayed after the explosion of the space shuttle Challenger over the Atlantic Ocean in 1986.)

A few years after the space mission, Mr. Akiyama left journalism and started working as a shiitake mushroom farmer, and taught agriculture and ethics at the Kyoto University of the Arts.

In addition to his wife, whom he married in 1999, Mr. Akiyama is survived by three children and a granddaughter.

Mr. Akiyama defended his reporting on the mission in the 1992 biography, saying that he saw himself as a medium for information about life in space and did not see the point of dwelling on his personal experience.

“Fundamentally, this project wasn’t about me personally achieving something extraordinary,” he said. “It was just a matter of chance.”

item.title: A Succession Battle Erupts Over a Late Ugandan Monarch
item.description:
A TV anchor. A young, mysterious heir. An amateur soccer player nicknamed “Big G.” Those were the people offered as candidates for the throne of the Tooro Kingdom in Uganda, after its former boy king died of cancer at age 34 last month.

The monarch, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, has not been laid to rest yet, but family members and royal clan leaders are locked in a highly public dispute over who should take his place. The conflict has ignited fears of a protracted succession battle for a powerful cultural institution in the East African country.

Uganda’s centuries-old kingdoms were outlawed by the government in 1967 when the president at the time sought to consolidate his rule. King Oyo’s father, who had just ascended to the throne, was forced into exile to Kenya. But four kingdoms — Buganda, Ankole, Bunyoro and Tooro — were reinstated in 1995, more as cultural institutions than political powers. King Oyo’s father returned to the country.

The father soon died, however, and the toddler Oyo was crowned that same year. Growing up, he went to school and played video games and soccer, and his mother controlled the household spending. (Women are barred from reigning in the kingdom, putting King Oyo before his mother and older sister in the line of succession.)

The young ruler was not known to have married. But in a statement about King Oyo’s death, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, prime minister of the Tooro Kingdom, announced for the first time that the late monarch had left an heir. He also said the son’s “identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time.”

President Yoweri Museveni of Uganda repeated the claim that King Oyo had left a “young boy heir.” And in social media statements he praised the king’s legacy, saying the young monarch had avoided the mistake of using his cultural power to “promote sectarianism.”

But on Wednesday, a 21-member succession committee from the royal clan of Tooro, called the Babiito, instead named as the king’s successor a prince turned TV anchor for the state broadcaster, UBC: Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma.

In 2015, the same anchor challenged King Oyo’s rule, questioning the monarch’s competence and asserting himself as a replacement, local news outlets reported.

The succession committee also considered nominating George Desmond Kamurasi, a cousin of King Oyo’s. Known as Big G, Mr. Kamurasi lives in London, where he is a content creator and amateur soccer player. But an elder on the committee, Charles Oyo, a Catholic priest, said in a local news interview that Mr. Kamurasi had declined the offer because “he has other responsibilities he has to undertake.”

On the same day that the committee announced Prince Edward, the late king’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, held her own news conference. She rejected the appointment of the TV anchor as her brother’s successor, saying the elders had gone behind the family’s back and caused “unnecessary drama.”

“It is very unfortunate that we have not even buried my brother yet, and they’re bringing all this confusion and all this turmoil,” she said. “We can’t even bury my brother in peace.”

On an official social media account, the Tooro Kingdom posted a portion of what it identified as the king’s 2022 will, in which he said he should be succeeded by a “lawfully recognized” biological son — if he had one. If not, the document listed two cousins as those next in line.

The king’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, said in a statement on Thursday that the same Babiito clan leaders, whom she said were “self-appointed,” had tried to interfere with King Oyo’s coronation when he was 3 years old.

She also said that a general in command of Uganda’s armed forces, Kayanja Muhanga, had removed the Tooro Palace’s royal guards and had deployed troops in their place. “We are under house arrest,” she said.

The Uganda People’s Defense Forces did not respond to a request for comment about the queen’s statement.

Mr. Armstrong, the kingdom’s prime minister, said on social media Thursday that the parties should take time to examine the laws and customs to resolve the dispute — after the king was buried.

The kingdom and the Queen Mother’s charitable foundation did not respond to requests for comment.“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our King still awaits burial,” he said.

King Oyo will be buried on Saturday in Fort Portal, the seat of the Tooro Kingdom near Uganda’s border with the Democratic Republic of Congo. The identify of his young boy heir is still a mystery.

item.title: Carney, at a Cabinet Retreat, Considers Further Trade Strikes Against the U.S.
item.description:
When Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada gathers his cabinet in Banff, Alberta, on Thursday, two questions are likely to loom over the semiannual retreat: whether the country should keep answering President Trump’s trade retaliation with more tariffs of its own, and how to help the hardest-hit businesses and workers.

On Tuesday, Canada retaliated against 50 percent American tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods with 15, 25 and 50 percent tariffs, depending on the product. The moves followed the collapse of trade talks last month between the once-close allies and put the countries, Mr. Carney said, “at war.”

Mr. Trump responded that evening by adding more products to his 50 percent tariff list and banning the imports of several Canadian goods outright, including beer, wine and liquor.

Mr. Carney has not spoken publicly since that escalation. Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for trade, said in a statement on social media that the government was “assessing” Mr. Trump’s latest blow to Canada’s economy.

He added: “As has been the case for the last 18 months, our first priority remains on protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from these unjustified actions.”

Polls released in recent days show unusually widespread support across Canada’s fractious regions for Mr. Carney’s decision to hit back, with many respondents wanting the government to go further — with measures like an export tax on electricity.

But Mr. Carney, a former central banker with a doctorate in economics, has not shown the same enthusiasm for tariffs as Doug Ford, Ontario’s premier. Mr. Carney seemed ambivalent about counter tariffs during the period after Canada’s new tariffs took effect but before Mr. Trump retaliated. “I don’t believe in escalating the conflict, that’s not constructive,” he said in a recorded video address to Canadians.

Since entering politics last year, Mr. Carney has not spoken about counter tariffs the way most economists might. But there is a broad consensus in that profession that Canada’s relatively small economy cannot meaningfully hurt the United States, while retaliatory tariffs raise prices for Canadians. Since Mr. Trump’s return to office, it has been clear that Canadian retaliation only provokes more reprisals from the White House.

None of that will matter at the cabinet table, said Andrew McDougall, an assistant professor of Canadian politics at the University of Toronto.

“Carney is as much a prisoner of public opinion now as he is a leader of it,” Professor McDougall said. “Public opinion right now is so inflamed that anything that looks like a concession or a walk back means that he’s going to get destroyed in the public eye.”

Earlier in the week, Mr. Trump had signaled he would ban entry of a particularly high-value Canadian export: business jets, largely built in Ontario and Quebec by Montreal-based Bombardier.

He settled instead for a smaller target made by a company also controlled by Bombardier’s founding family. Starting Sept. 29, the United States will bar three-wheeled motorcycles made in Quebec by BRP, short for Bombardier Recreational Products, best known for Ski-Doo snowmobiles and, like its sister aerospace company, a symbol of the province’s industrial prowess.

The ban appears to be retaliation for a 50 percent Canadian tariff on American motorcycles that threatens to price Harley-Davidson out of the Canadian market.

Emilie Proulx, a spokeswoman for BRP, said the ban will have limited effect in the near term because the company has already shipped the “vast majority” of motorcycles ordered by American dealers for this season.

The import ban also covers nearly every type of beer, wine and liquor, including alcohol-free beer, a response to eight of Canada’s 10 provinces pulling American products from government liquor stores and distribution systems. Mr. Ford and his British Columbia counterpart, David Eby, have set a high bar for any trade agreement that would let them reverse course.

Also newly banned: various forms of whey, the liquid left over after cheese and yogurt making, now in high demand for protein supplements.

Mr. Trump has long made exaggerated and misleading claims about Canada’s restrictions on American dairy imports.

Aluminum products were added to the 50 percent tariff list, along with furniture, motorboats longer than 7.5 meters, several paper products, mattresses and golf carts — expanding on the steel, aluminum and auto tariffs imposed last year that helped sink the trade talks.

The White House did lift tariffs on some goods, including tissue used for toilet paper and facial tissue, paper bedsheets, road salt, lead, “chemically pure sugars,” some electrical equipment and fishing rods.

Wendong Zhang, a professor of economics at Cornell University, said his model that tracks the effects of the tariffs launched during the trade war confirms that Canada’s retaliation causes more economic harm than restraint would — but that Ottawa has chosen its targets carefully. Butter, the largest U.S. dairy export to Canada, is absent.

Professor Zhang added that the effects of tariffs can linger long after they’re lifted. Saskatchewan and Alberta briefly banned American liquor early in the trade war, and sales remain down by more than 60 percent since the products were returned to shelves.

Still, Professor Zhang expects Mr. Carney to announce further retaliation.

“I understand that it’s politically suicidal to not have a reaction,” he said.

item.title: Gander Welcomed Americans in 2001. Now, U.S.-Canada Tensions Hit Home.
item.description:
If any small town ever embodied Canada’s traditionally rock-solid friendship with the United States, Gander was it.

Gander — just inland on the island of Newfoundland — was where generations of U.S. soldiers made their last stop in North America before venturing across the Atlantic to conflicts from World War II to Iran. Where many Canadians and Americans forged friendships and even marriages over the decades.

And where residents took care of thousands of stranded and frightened airline passengers after the Sept. 11 attacks, inspiring the tale of selfless humanity and deep cross-border ties in the hit musical, “Come from Away.”

“We were the best ally they ever had,” said Beulah Cooper, 85, a Gander resident whose real-life bond with Hannah O’Rourke, a New Yorker whose firefighter son was killed in the World Trade Center’s North Tower, forms the musical’s emotional core. She paused, considering current tensions with the United States and added, “It’s — it’s hurtful when you stop and think about it.”

While Gander commemorates the Sept. 11 attacks every year, the event planned for Friday is taking place amid an extraordinary deterioration in relations between Canada and the United States that began with President Trump’s second term and grows more intense by the week. Even as the people in Gander recalled the lifelong friendships with Americans that resulted from the events in 2001, a strong undercurrent of hurt, disappointment and anger has run through the preparations for the 25th commemoration.

“It would be foolish to suggest that stuff is not running in the background,” said Percy Farwell, the mayor of Gander and deputy mayor during the attacks. “But that’s not what we are remembering on Sept. 11. It’s not about the relationship between our two governments or who’s got the biggest trade surplus. We’re talking about humans that we have a lot in common with.”

Still, in an hourlong interview at town hall, Mr. Farwell spoke about his disappointment at the Trump administration’s treatment of Canada.

“We’re polite, and we’re your best friend until you betray us, or threaten us, or insult us, or disrespect us,” he said. “And then we have a pretty strong resolve.”

The deep ambivalence in Gander — ahead of a two-day ceremony involving high-ranking Canadian and U.S. officials, emergency workers, community leaders and passengers from the stranded aircraft — is a microcosm of how the United States’ place in the world and its relations with its closest allies have changed in the past quarter of a century. After the attacks, the United States received an outpouring of sympathy from much of the world.

Last month, after a breakdown in trade talks, Prime Minister Mark Carney described the United States as posing a danger to Canada’s sovereignty and economy. President Trump warned Canadian leaders to “fall in line.”

In his second term, Mr. Trump launched a trade war against Canada, and he threatened to annex Canada and turn it into the 51st state. He has kept up a stream of insults against Canadian leaders and institutions — echoed by members of his cabinet and the U.S. ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, who is slated to attend the commemoration in Gander.

The breakdown in relations and the escalating trade war have left both Canadians and Americans bewildered.

“I’m angry at our government’s rhetoric and actions — this is not the way you treat your neighbor, period,” Kevin Tuerff, an American whose experience of being stranded in Gander with his partner is told in the musical, said by phone from New York City. “Canadians didn’t just help America on 9-11. They’ve helped us in multiple wars we dragged them into.”

“Honestly, I’m embarrassed,” said Mr. Tuerff, 60, who is scheduled to participate in the upcoming commemoration in Gander.

Moved by the generosity of the people in Gander in the days after the Sept. 11 attacks, Mr. Tuerff founded Pay It Forward 9/11, a charity that encourages acts of kindness on the anniversary. One example has stayed with him a quarter of a century later: He and others sheltered at a college in Gander were allowed to freely make long-distance phone calls.

“So we said, ‘Can we give you some money?’” he recalled. “‘No, no, you would do the same,’ they said. And I thought: Would we?”

Even before 2001, Gander’s airport had played a prominent role in the history of aviation. Canada, the British and Newfoundland built the airport in 1938 in the middle of the wilderness but, critically, along the shortest flight path across the Atlantic on the most eastern landmass in North America, with the exception of Greenland. During World War II, the United States helped expand the facility into one of the largest military air bases in the world. The airport’s largest section was known as the “American Side” — complete with hangars, accommodations, a bowling alley and a movie theater.

A suburban-style, car-friendly town created to service the airport — with large thoroughfares like “Airport Boulevard,” residential crescents named after aviators, few sidewalks and no historic core — grew next to the airport.

The airport itself served as a refueling stop for commercial aircraft after the war. After jets started flying nonstop across the Atlantic in the 1960s, the airport continued to serve as a stop for U.S. military aircraft and an emergency stop for commercial planes.

“Gander has always been a safe haven for anything that happens on the Eastern Seaboard,” said Dion Faulkner, who oversees the operations in Canada for Allied Aviation, a New York-based company that services carriers at airports in North and Central America.

So shortly after the attacks on the morning of Sept. 11 — with U.S. airspace closed — international flights, most en route to the United States, were diverted to Canadian airports. The 38 planes and 6,700 passengers landing at Gander nearly doubled the town’s population.

The planes waited on the tarmac between eight and 24 hours before passengers were allowed to disembark, Mr. Faulkner said.

“We had to go to the local drugstore to get Nicorette, baby formula, diapers, and we started putting that on the planes,” Mr. Faulkner said.

If disembarking passengers were frightened, so, too, were the locals who feared that terrorists could be aboard.

“Who are we letting in here? Who are we going to put in amongst these innocent people?” recalled thinking Betty Moulton, who, as a volunteer with the Red Cross, greeted passengers into the airport’s international terminal.

Nevertheless, countless people in Gander rallied to help.

“We never had to ask for volunteers,” recalled Claude Elliott, the mayor at the time. “People came in, people wanted to help. It was volunteers who stayed there 24 hours around the clock to make sure that passengers were taken care of.”

Passengers were sheltered in schools, churches and many private homes.

Learning that many were staying at her daughter’s school, Dawn Baker took over sanitary pads, sleeping bags and visited repeatedly with salad bowls. A stranded teenage girl stayed in her basement, watching movies for days before she was able to fly out to New York.

Being able to help “was a gift for all of us here,” Ms. Baker said. “We were all watching it on television, and you felt this hopelessness that there’s nothing you can do. But there was something we could do, so we hopped up and did it.”

Raphael Fusco was 17 years old and flying back to New Jersey with his father. Like all other passengers, they had to leave their luggage on the plane.

“We had no idea what was going on, we were distraught,” recalled Mr. Fusco, a composer and pianist, in a phone interview. “And these people, they gave us toothbrushes, toothpaste, they took us bowling. They made us feel like family and gave everything of themselves.”

“So when the whole world was seeing unspeakable acts of violence, the only thing that we saw was how good people could be,” Mr. Fusco said.

Mr. Fusco said he was “embarrassed” by the U.S. government’s current “bullying” of Canada. “It just shows a lack of gratitude, a lack of respect,” he said. “It just bothers me so much to see the opposite of what the Canadians showed us in terms of generosity and hospitality and warmness and brotherhood.”

Tony Toluba, a Virginia resident, is planning to come to Gander for the 25th anniversary on what will be his third visit after being stranded in 2001. He was aware that relations between the two nations are now very different from what they were during his previous visits.

“I don’t know what it will actually be like when I get there, I do have a little bit of trepidation,” Mr. Toluba said in a phone interview. “But the thing that struck me most about Newfoundland is that they’re very friendly, they’re very people oriented. I think on a people level, I think I will have the same kind of experience I’ve had in the past. At least, I certainly hope that I will.”

item.title: U.K. Sanctions on Israeli Settlements in West Bank Divide British Rabbis
item.description:
Britain’s sanctions against Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank have sparked public division among British rabbis, with many framing their reaction in terms of their own fears about threats against Jews in Britain.

Several rabbis expressed support for the sanctions and spoke about violence they had witnessed or personally experienced from extremist settlers in the West Bank. At the same time, the country’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of Britain’s Orthodox Jews, was among several prominent Jews who condemned the move.

Such conflicting statements — coming days before the holiest period in the Jewish calendar — are among the most public signs of the deep divisions among British Jews, who have faced a series of violent attacks in recent months.

“Nobody should ever suggest that they represent the single opinion of any group of Jews anywhere,” said Rabbi Jeremy Gordon, who published a letter on Wednesday supporting the sanctions and detailing his own experiences with settlers.

But while British Jews have varied opinions on both Israeli and British politics, he said, almost none support or condone the violence. “There are very, very few people who would associate themselves with the extreme far right in Israel,” he said.

The sanctions, jointly announced with Canada and France, ban trade in settlement goods, and a dozen countries in all supported them.

In response, Israel’s foreign minister said the sanctions were based on “outrageous lies,” ordered the British Consulate in Jerusalem closed and barred from Israel a dozen British lawmakers and others he deemed anti-Israeli and antisemitic.

The sanctions come at a tense time for Britain, Israel and the West Bank. International attention is focused on Israel’s tightening grip on the enclave and its expansion of settlements there. In recent weeks, settlers have repeatedly attacked Palestinians as the Israeli military has stood by.

Britain, a longtime ally of Israel, has condemned the West Bank settlements, which are considered illegal under international law. The sanctions represent a striking escalation of its criticism. They come after British Jews have faced a recent wave of antisemitic attacks.

In October, two Jews died in Manchester in an attack on their synagogue during Yom Kippur. In March, arsonists destroyed ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer service in London. In April, two men were stabbed in a Jewish area of London, in what British officials called a terrorist attack.

In July, the British government accused an arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of almost certainly directing some of those attacks.

Many British Jews have wrestled with how to reconcile the attacks with outrage over Israel’s support of the settlements and its war in Gaza, in which tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed. The war was set off by the Hamas-led attacks in 2023, which killed about 1,200 people.

Some argue that any anti-Israel statements or actions by the British government can lead to violence against Jews.

“These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target,” Britain’s chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, said on social media on Tuesday.

He said Britain’s Jews were “more vulnerable than ever” and argued that the sanctions add to the danger they face.

“Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews,” he added.

Some British Jews argue that Israel’s policies have made them less safe, as those angry with the Israeli government could misdirect their rage against Jews and Jewish sites in Britain.

“Part of the reason why this is happening — this isn’t to condone it — is because terrible things are being said by people who are condoning and inflaming the West Bank settlers who are violently attacking Palestinians in the West Bank,” said Rabbi Gordon.

He and several others couched their support for the sanctions in terms of their own experiences in the West Bank.

Rabbi Jonathan Wittenberg, who leads the Masorti Jewish communities in Britain (which is similar to the conservative communities in the United States), said in a letter posted on social media on Wednesday that he had spent time this week in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair in the West Bank.

There, he said, he met a man whose brother had been killed by a settler 13 months ago. The settler violence “is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order,” he wrote.

He described a village “under siege,” saying that he had met families who could not reach their livestock or access the toilet. The Israeli authorities defend the settlers, he said, not the villagers.

“It desecrates the millennia-old good name of the Jewish People,” he continued. “It prepares the way for more and yet more conflict, suffering and grief.”

Britain’s move drew criticism from the U.S. ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who warned the sanctions could stoke tensions with Washington and, potentially, a U.S. response.

As in Britain, the settlements and Israel have proved intensively divisive among American Jews, and Mr. Huckabee, an evangelical Christian, has himself condemned settler violence.

item.title: Ancient Tombs, Untouched by Looters, Are Found Under Peru’s Sands
item.description:
Under a ruined citadel on Peru’s arid northern coast, archaeologists have discovered an ancient mausoleum untouched by centuries of conquest and plunder by the Inca, Spanish colonizers, and generations of looters, officials announced this week.

The site, Chan Chan, whose ruins include giant adobe brick ruins, has been excavated for decades. But researchers had never before found an undisturbed tomb at the city, which was the capital of the Chimu kingdom that ruled much of Peru’s coast before the Inca.

The tombs contained 38 bodies, archaeologists said, adding that the scale of the mausoleum — nearly 55 feet on each side and 16 feet high — and the scores of artifacts within suggest the people buried there were members of the Chimu elite. The team of Peruvian archaeologists said that the tombs were about 600 years old, which would date them to just before or during the Inca conquest of the region, in the mid-1400s.

“This is the discovery of the decade in terms of it’s the very first time that, as archaeologists, we are able to see an elite Chimu burial,” said Gabriel Prieto, a professor of anthropology at the University of Florida, who was not involved in the research.

The Peruvian archaeologists realized only slowly that they had found something different, as they removed sand, soil and debris from the tomb’s entrance one centimeter at a time.

“It was a feeling of anxiety and urgency, to know if we were really in front of a chamber that had never been looted,” said Jorge Meneses, the archaeologist responsible for excavations.

By the time they had cleared about 40 centimeters from the door, he said, the team could peer inside with a flashlight. They saw a series of funerary bundles, still safe from thieves after hundreds of years.

“In that moment we realized that the chamber had not been looted,” he said.

The excavation, near the town of Trujillo, has taken months and is still going on. It has revealed a stairway that descends eight feet into the middle of the mausoleum, where one chamber is flanked on each side by a larger room. One person was buried in the central chamber; the eastern room was nearly empty; and the western room held a trove of artifacts and the remains of about 20 people. Eighteen more have been found elsewhere in the complex.

The skeletal remains in the central chamber had red pigment on the skull and some other bones, Dr. Meneses said, as did two skeletons atop the funeral platform. Archaeologists say the pigment may be cinnabar, another clue suggesting the remains were from the Chimu elite.

Many of the remains had ear ornaments, silver- or copper-plated necklaces, or jewelry made of quartz, shells and semiprecious stones. The researchers also found a large number of metal weapons, heavy beads and a wooden chest containing colorful textiles decorated with images of seabirds and monkeys.

“It’s really like a treasure chest,” Dr. Prieto said.

He said that the design of the tombs and evidence from Chimu art suggests that the mausoleums were “designed to be open.” Chimu people would go in and out, he said, depositing bodies or offerings and taking human remains “out of those burials to be placed on plazas and venerated as ancestors.”

The discovery raises many questions, archaeologists said, and could significantly bolster knowledge about the Chimu. At about nine square miles, Chan Chan was the biggest city of the Americas in its time, with gardens, plazas, pyramids and mausoleums. The tomb could shed light on Chimu practices as well as on their relations with the Inca and other cultures to the north and south.

The Peruvian authorities said the bodies were still being analyzed, and have not yet revealed any details about the dead, including ages, sex, where they were born or how they may have died. (Nearly 140 child skeletons and the remains of 200 llamas were found at another Chimu site in 2019, possibly in an act of mass human sacrifice during a disastrous El Niño.)

“What is clear to us so far is that these people were part of the elite or were associated with the elite,” said Henry Luis Gayoso, the head of the project at Chan Chan and an official in Peru’s Ministry of Culture.

The excavation could provide a wealth of information to archaeologists about a transformative moment in the ancient Americas as one kingdom faced off with a rising empire, said Robyn Cutright, an anthropologist at Centre College who was not involved in the research.

The bodies, the objects and the design of the mausoleum itself could offer clues about how the Chimu and the Inca interacted. While museums and collections around the world hold Chimu objects, including those that appear to be from royal tombs, “this really is a great opportunity to see something we haven’t see before, a royal tomb undisturbed at Chan Chan,” she said.

“You can see something cool in a museum that a looter sold to a collector,” she said, “but this is the real meat of how archaeologists tell stories.”

item.title: The Death of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s Child Changed Her View of Nigeria
item.description:
The writer Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and her husband were spending the holidays at their home in Lagos, Nigeria, last December when one of their twin sons came down with what seemed to be a cold. The child, Nkanu, was 21 months old — “precious” and “a funny baby,” in the words of his father, Ivara Esege. He was still playful, but when he developed a fever, Esege, who is a physician, started him on antibiotics.

By New Year’s Day, Nkanu had not improved, so the couple took him to a local children’s hospital. Concerned that he might have atypical Kawasaki disease, a childhood illness that can lead to heart attacks and strokes, Esege also contacted Johns Hopkins Hospital, near the couple’s American home in suburban Maryland. Johns Hopkins agreed to take Nkanu as a patient, but doctors there asked for additional tests to make sure he was safe to travel. Adichie and Esege took Nkanu to Euracare, another hospital in Lagos, for the examination.

The child was sedated with Propofol, a common anesthetic, to keep him still during an M.R.I. of his brain. Adichie was waiting outside when a doctor hurried past her into the cath lab. It was alarming: Why was he rushing to the room where Nkanu was having his test done? She waited in “pure panic,” she said, until the doctor returned. “He was very calm and he said to me, ‘Well, look, they gave him too much Propofol,’” Adichie recalled. “Those were his exact words, which I will never forget until the day I die.”

Nkanu had gone into cardiac arrest. Within 24 hours — it is not clear exactly when — he was dead.

Adichie and Esege told me this story in July, at their home in Maryland. On the table, there was a tray of healthy snacks: bowls of fresh cherries, another bowl of seeds and dried fruit. Adichie, 48, was dressed in a plain, loosefitting dress, her hair combed into two simple braids. Esege, tall with a curly salt-and-pepper Afro, wore a yellow T-shirt and gym shorts. He is 57 and, like his wife, a native of Nigeria.

There was an easy choreography between the couple, but also a palpable weariness. Leading me to the dining room, where we spoke for several hours, they moved slowly, as if bereavement were a kind of arthritis, pain carried in the bones. The house was more than quiet. Their daughter, age 10, was at day camp, and the younger of the twin boys was upstairs, sleeping. (The couple asked The New York Times not to use their children’s names to protect their privacy.)

Adichie and Esege still struggle to understand how their child could have died so suddenly and inexplicably. They have urged a coroner’s court to conduct an inquest — and the court is doing so — in hopes that they can help other Nigerians who have been harmed by the country’s troubled health care system but lack the means and influence to push for change. They stress that they are not suing the hospital or the doctors and just want a better health care system.

“That’s the only thing we can try and do just to help,” Esege told me. “Hopefully someone else will not have to go through this.”

The pain of Nkanu’s death has complicated Adichie’s relationship with Nigeria. The country, with its mix of resilience, vibrancy, corruption and economic desperation, is a vivid milieu in her work, exerting a strong magnetic pull on characters who leave.

In her best-known novel, “Americanah,” the main character, Ifemelu, is a young Nigerian woman who, much like the author, comes to the United States to study and live, only to experience exhaustion and alienation that feels like “cement in her soul.” Nigeria, Adichie writes, was “where she was supposed to be, the only place she could sink her roots in without the constant urge to tug them out and shake off the soil.”

Now Adichie feels uprooted. “My feelings toward Nigeria have changed,” she said. Her son’s death was the first irrevocable loss, her native country the second.

Health care in Nigeria suffers from relatively low government support, limited infrastructure and an exodus of skilled workers. According to a recent estimate from the World Bank, Nigeria has 0.4 doctors for every 1,000 people (the figure is 3.7 in the United States).

But Adichie said she had confidence in Euracare, which she was told was run by international standards. “It was kind of paraded as one of the best hospitals in Lagos,” she explained.

As it happened, she knew the doctor who spoke to her outside the cath lab. His name was Tosin Majekodunmi, and she had met him while accompanying her parents to their annual checkups at Euracare.

“My father liked him very much,” Adichie said. “I did come to consider him a friend. When my father died, he was very kind and called me.”

According to Adichie, Dr. Majekodunmi told her the doctors had saved Nkanu and he was now stable: “He said, ‘But everything is OK now because we got him back.’ And I kind of felt — I felt really confused.”

She shook her head and spoke more slowly, her voice thick with tears. “I trusted him,” she said.

Dr. Majekodunmi did not respond to interview requests from The Times.

The night Nkanu fell ill, she went home to gather the documents and payments necessary to transport him back to the United States the next morning in an air ambulance. She left and Esege stayed at the hospital.

Esege, who retired from his work as a family physician in Baltimore when the twins were born, was still at the hospital when he looked at the report the hospital’s staff had prepared for the air ambulance company. He was shocked to see that it said Nkanu’s pupils were fixed and dilated. And on the Blantyre coma scale the doctors had marked their son at zero in a range of one to five, meaning he had shown no eye movement and didn’t respond to pain.

Egese’s voice cracked as he described his reaction to me: “Nobody said anything to me about this. I mean, this basically means Nkanu is gone.”

Not dead yet, but lacking any meaningful brain function. Esege said he believed, based on the report, that Dr. Majekodunmi knew Nkanu was beyond saving after the first cardiac arrest, but he didn’t want to tell Adichie because of his closeness to her and her family.

Esege said the doctor had urged him not to call Adichie until the hospital could do a CT scan, but he replied that he couldn’t keep the information from her. He texted his wife and asked her to come back, and she returned around midnight. In the next few hours, Nkanu’s heart stopped at least two more times.

“So they basically are doing cardiac resuscitations on this poor boy for more than four hours, until 8 in the morning, when they decided to call it,” Egese said. “Nkanu, our son, was gone.”

It seemed that Esege’s theory about the timing of Nkanu’s death was not one he had shared with his wife. Adichie looked at him, incredulous, and asked, “So, sorry. We don’t actually know when our son died?”

She paused and then said again, in disbelief, “We don’t know when he died.”

Turning to me, Adichie said, “I’m actually hearing this for the first time. Some of it.” She then referred to Esege by his nickname. “I didn’t know about IV’s conversation with the doctor when I went home to try to get the payments for the ambulance. I think IV’s tried to protect me.”

Near us in the dining room, Nkanu’s highchair was still at the table, next to his brother’s. His clothes were still folded upstairs in his room. Adichie mentioned that she now had to buy clothes for one boy, not two, but was still in the habit of adding two of every item — T-shirt, shorts, sweater — to the online shopping cart.

Intermittently, throughout our conversation, she took out her phone and showed me videos of Nkanu. For brief moments, there were echoes of his laughter. On the screen of his mother’s phone, Nkanu sang and danced, played with her jewelry and climbed on Esege’s back while he pretended to be a horse, galloping the child across imaginary fields.

Not long after Nkanu died, Adichie and Esege filed a complaint with the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria — a separate entity from the one conducting the inquest — and in February the council announced an initial finding of negligence on the part of three physicians: Dr. Majekodunmi; Dr. Titus Ogundare, the anesthesiologist who sedated Nkanu; and a doctor from Atlantis Pediatric Hospital, where Nkanu was first treated. The three were suspended pending a formal hearing; the Atlantis physician has since been cleared.

Dr. Ogundare did not respond to requests for comment.

The coroner’s inquest itself has turned into a battle, with Adichie accusing Euracare of playing a “monstrous cynical game” by creating unnecessary delays. (The inquest has been delayed until the fall.) When Esege joined an inquest hearing remotely in June, Euracare shocked the couple by accusing them of a crime: destroying evidence by having their son cremated. According to local news reports, the hospital’s lawyer, Taiwo Osipitan, said: “What they did is punishable by 15 years imprisonment. The issue is whether somebody who has done something wrong under the law can push for an inquest.”

Sylvester Shih, Euracare’s chief operating officer, did not respond to a request for comment.

“I feel so bad for IV,” Adichie said. “He’s on Zoom. He’s hearing it all. He’s hearing when someone is saying that he destroyed evidence, and by evidence, they mean our child.”

Even before Nkanu’s death, Adichie and Esege were adjusting to the losses of both of her parents and Esege’s brother in recent years. She recalled a conversation she had with her husband on Jan. 7, the day after Nkanu died.

“I just remember looking at IV and saying, ‘Do we have to have another funeral?’ IV said, ‘I cannot.’ And IV said, ‘We’ll cremate him. We’ll take him with us because we can’t leave him behind.’”

Along with her four novels Adichie has given popular TED talks and published short fiction, essays, children’s literature and, after her father’s death in 2020, a book called “Notes on Grief.”

“When my father died, I was struck by the physicality of grief. And this time, even more so,” she told me. “I feel it. It’s in my stomach and it’s in my chest, and you’re just so tired every day. Everything is difficult. Everything. And then you have to pretend. You have to pretend because you have children, and you’re terrified of how they’re doing. Sometimes my son doesn’t want me to hold him because I’m so weepy. He’s 2. So I really try. It feels like the full manifestation of my grief is impossible because of the condition of being a mother.”

About then, the little boy woke up with a wail and Esege went upstairs to get him.

Later, he swept into the room, his sister’s sweater draped over his shoulders like a superhero’s cape. He crawled into the cradle of his mother’s lap until he saw that his father had a soccer ball and went tearing after it. It was the week of the World Cup semifinals and the family found the games to be an engaging distraction.

Then the front door opened and the couple’s daughter bounced in. Tall like her father, she was dressed in all pink, her favorite color. She whispered something to her mother and Adichie smiled. Monday is hamburger day and her daughter wanted to make sure that even though she had eaten a burger over the weekend, she would get to have her favorite American meal because it was still Monday.

When we talked, Adichie had not been back to the country of her birth, the place she has brought to life in novels beloved by millions of readers, in six months. She had mentioned that she and Esege were planning to return there soon, and I asked if they planned to take their son and daughter with them. They have taught their children to love Nigeria even as they learn about its structural and political challenges.

Adichie grimaced and said, “They’re the reason we’re going.”

“Really, we’ve had two homes forever,” she continued. “We were in Nigeria every Christmas, every Easter, every summer. Our daughter said to me recently, ‘Mama, Nigeria is my happy place.’ She’s the one who wants to go.’”

I asked what her little boy understood about all that had happened. She shook her head and said, “He always says his brother is in Lagos.”

Adichie said she had always loved Nigeria and felt grateful to have a home there and one in Maryland. She came to the United States at 19 to study at Drexel University in Philadelphia and went on to earn master’s degrees from Johns Hopkins and Yale.

“I think that America made it possible for me to write, which is my life’s vocation,” she said. “But Nigeria gave me everything I needed to be able to write. And I feel grateful for that.”

But is Nigeria still where she is supposed to be?

She wiped the tears from her face and continued: “I mean, it is so surreal, all of this. I still can’t believe we’re talking about my son who died. You’re going through something, but you also feel like you’re outside of it.”

After a moment she said softly, “I do not want to go back to Nigeria.”

I came to this story with some experience of having a child who needed intensive medical care. When I wrote to Adichie and Esege about an interview, I let them know that I was a journalist but also a mother who spent four months in the NICU with my child.A few weeks later, I traveled to their home in Baltimore where the couple sat together, it turns out for the first time, and went hour by hour through the last night of their son’s life.

Deborah Segun (b. 1994) is a multidisciplinary artist from Lagos, Nigeria, based in London.
